claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry and in vitro kinase assays presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Depletion of ERK3 prevented both basal and EGF-dependent RAC1 and CDC42 activation.
claims.source: Consistently, depletion of ERK3 prevented both basal and EGF-dependent RAC1 and CDC42 activation, maintenance of F-actin content, filopodia formation, and epithelial cell migration.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Depletion of ERK3 prevented maintenance of F-actin content.
claims.source: Consistently, depletion of ERK3 prevented both basal and EGF-dependent RAC1 and CDC42 activation, maintenance of F-actin content, filopodia formation, and epithelial cell migration.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from F/G-actin assays shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Depletion of ERK3 prevented filopodia formation.
claims.source: Consistently, depletion of ERK3 prevented both basal and EGF-dependent RAC1 and CDC42 activation, maintenance of F-actin content, filopodia formation, and epithelial cell migration.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from confocal and SEM imaging shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Depletion of ERK3 prevented epithelial cell migration.
claims.source: Consistently, depletion of ERK3 prevented both basal and EGF-dependent RAC1 and CDC42 activation, maintenance of F-actin content, filopodia formation, and epithelial cell migration.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell tracking and migration assays shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: ERK3 protein bound directly to the purified ARP2/3 complex.
claims.source: Further, ERK3 protein bound directly to the purified ARP2/3 complex and augmented polymerization of actin in vitro.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from GST pull-down and ELISA assays shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: ERK3 augmented polymerization of actin in vitro.
claims.source: Further, ERK3 protein bound directly to the purified ARP2/3 complex and augmented polymerization of actin in vitro.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pyrene-actin polymerization assays shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: ERK3 kinase activity was required for the formation of actin-rich protrusions in mammalian cells.
claims.source: ERK3 kinase activity was required for the formation of actin-rich protrusions in mammalian cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from complementation experiments with kinase-dead ERK3 shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Actin is one of the most abundant and highly conserved proteins with over 95% homology among all isoforms.
claims.source: Actin is one of the most abundant and highly conserved proteins with over 95% homology among all isoforms (Vandekerckhove and Weber, 1979).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vandekerckhove and Weber, 1979.

claims.claim: In cells, actin is present in globular/monomeric form (G-actin), which can polymerize into branched and elongated filamentous forms (F-actin).
claims.source: In cells, it is present in globular/monomeric form (G-actin), which can polymerize into branched and elongated filamentous forms (F-actin) in a dynamic, spatially, and temporally controlled process (Skruber et al., 2018; Lee and Dominguez, 2010; Carlsson, 2006; Carlier et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: The cytoplasmic actin network regulates velocity and directionality of cell migration.
claims.source: It regulates velocity and directionality of cell migration, enables intracellular signaling and transport, supports cell division, and more (Yamaguchi and Condeelis, 2007; dos Remedios et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yamaguchi and Condeelis, 2007 and dos Remedios et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The actin cytoskeleton can form unique structures such as lamellipodia and filopodia.
claims.source: Moreover, by branching and bundling of F-actin filaments the actin cytoskeleton can form unique structures such as lamellipodia and filopodia, which in epithelial cells regulate cell polarization and are crucial for the contact with their environment, while in other cell types these actin rich structures control motility, chemotaxis, and haptotaxis (Vasioukhin et al., 2000; Raich et al., 1999; Millard and Martin, 2008; Khurana and George, 2011; Bahri et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claims.claim: The spatiotemporally defined branching and elongation of the polymerized actin filaments is achieved by activation of nucleation factors including the ARP2/3 complex, formins, and spire.
claims.source: The spatiotemporally defined branching and elongation of the polymerized actin filaments is achieved by activation of nucleation factors including the Actin-related protein 2 and 3 (ARP2/3) complex, formins, and spire (Rouiller et al., 2008; Rohatgi et al., 1999; Carlier et al., 1999; Chesarone and Goode, 2009; Campellone and Welch, 2010; Pollard, 2007; Schuldt, 2005; Buracco et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claims.claim: ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization generates branched F-actin network.
claims.source: It is well established that ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization generates branched F-actin network, while formins generate unbranched filaments and promote growth of actin filaments at the barbed end (Pollard, 2007; Wood and Martin, 2002; Yang and Svitkina, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pollard, 2007; Wood and Martin, 2002; Yang and Svitkina, 2011.

claims.claim: Formins generate unbranched filaments and promote growth of actin filaments at the barbed end.
claims.source: It is well established that ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization generates branched F-actin network, while formins generate unbranched filaments and promote growth of actin filaments at the barbed end (Pollard, 2007; Wood and Martin, 2002; Yang and Svitkina, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pollard, 2007; Wood and Martin, 2002; Yang and Svitkina, 2011.

claims.claim: ARP2/3 complex is a major and highly conserved actin nucleator composed of seven subunits.
claims.source: ARP2/3 complex is a major and highly conserved actin nucleator composed of seven subunits (Robinson et al., 2001; Goley and Welch, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Robinson et al., 2001 and Goley and Welch, 2006.

claims.claim: The activation of ARP2/3 complex relies on binding to pre-formed actin filament and nucleation-promoting factors (NPFs).
claims.source: The structural and biochemical properties of the ARP2/3 complex have been intensively studied in vitro, and apart from ATP, its activation relies on binding to pre-formed actin filament and nucleation-promoting factors (NPFs) (Robinson et al., 2001; Goley and Welch, 2006; Pizarro-Cerdá et al., 2017; Nolen et al., 2004; Nolen and Pollard, 2007; Espinoza-Sanchez et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claims.claim: The main regulators of the ARP2/3 complex belong to the Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) family proteins.
claims.source: The main regulators of the ARP2/3 complex belong to the Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) family proteins, including WASP-family verprolin-homologous protein (WAVE) (Yarar et al., 1999; Machesky et al., 1999; Higgs et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yarar et al., 1999; Machesky et al., 1999; Higgs et al., 1999.

claims.claim: WASP and WAVE proteins serve as a link between the actin cytoskeleton and RhoGTPases via direct and intermediate binding to CDC42 and RAC1, respectively.
claims.source: WASP and WAVE proteins serve as a link between the actin cytoskeleton and RhoGTPases via direct and intermediate binding to cell division control 42 (CDC42) and Ras-related C3 botulin toxin substrate 1 (RAC1), respectively (Rohatgi et al., 1999; Carlier et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rohatgi et al., 1999 and Carlier et al., 1999.

claims.claim: The small RhoGTPases function as binary molecular switches circulating between active (GTP-bound) and inactive (GDP-bound) state.
claims.source: They function as binary molecular switches circulating between active (GTP-bound) and inactive (GDP-bound) state.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about RhoGTPases.

claims.claim: The on-off regulation of the RhoGTPases is under the control of guanine exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs).
claims.source: The on-off regulation of the RhoGTPases is under the control of guanine exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) (Hodge and Ridley, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hodge and Ridley, 2016.

claims.claim: GTP-bound active CDC42 and RAC1 promote the formation of filopodia and lamellipodia, respectively.
claims.source: GTP-bound active CDC42 and RAC1 promote the formation of filopodia and lamellipodia, respectively, by activating the NPFs, WASP, and WAVE (Rohatgi et al., 1999; Carlier et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rohatgi et al., 1999 and Carlier et al., 1999.

claims.claim: Recent studies revealed a role for kinases in directly activating RhoGTPases mainly through phosphorylation.
claims.source: Recent studies revealed a role for kinases in directly activating RhoGTPases mainly through phosphorylation, but the identity of the relevant kinase(s) remained elusive (Tong et al., 2013; Forget et al., 2002; Chang et al., 2011; Tu et al., 2003; Ren et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: ERK3 (MAPK6) is an atypical member of the mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs).
claims.source: ERK3 (MAPK6) is an atypical member of the mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ERK3.

claims.claim: Kinase-dependent roles of ERK3 include promoting lung cancer cell migration and invasion.
claims.source: Its physiological roles are tissue-specific and can be both dependent and independent of its catalytic activity: kinase-dependent roles of ERK3 include promoting lung cancer cell migration and invasion, while its function in the regulation of breast cancer cell morphology and migration is shown to be partially kinase-independent (Al-Mahdi et al., 2015; Bogucka et al., 2021; Bogucka et al., 2020; Elkhadragy et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Al-Mahdi et al., 2015; Bogucka et al., 2021; Bogucka et al., 2020; Elkhadragy et al., 2020.

claims.claim: ERK3's function in the regulation of breast cancer cell morphology and migration is shown to be partially kinase-independent.
claims.source: Its physiological roles are tissue-specific and can be both dependent and independent of its catalytic activity: kinase-dependent roles of ERK3 include promoting lung cancer cell migration and invasion, while its function in the regulation of breast cancer cell morphology and migration is shown to be partially kinase-independent (Al-Mahdi et al., 2015; Bogucka et al., 2021; Bogucka et al., 2020; Elkhadragy et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Al-Mahdi et al., 2015; Bogucka et al., 2021; Bogucka et al., 2020; Elkhadragy et al., 2020.

claims.claim: ERK3 is a labile protein whose rapid turnover has been implicated in cellular differentiation.
claims.source: Moreover, ERK3 is a labile protein whose rapid turnover has been implicated in cellular differentiation (Bogucka et al., 2021; Coulombe et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bogucka et al., 2021 and Coulombe et al., 2003.

claims.claim: ERK3 possesses a single phosphorylation site at serine 189 (S189) within S-E-G activation motif.
claims.source: It is, however, known that ERK3 possesses a single phosphorylation site at serine 189 (S189) within S-E-G activation motif, located in its kinase domain, which was shown to be phosphorylated by group I p-21-activated kinases (PAKs), the direct effectors of RAC1 and CDC42 GTPases (Déléris et al., 2011; De la Mota-Peynado et al., 2011; Coulombe and Meloche, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Déléris et al., 2011; De la Mota-Peynado et al., 2011; Coulombe and Meloche, 2007.

claims.claim: ERK3 signaling is required for the motility and migration of different cancer cells.
claims.source: ERK3 signaling is required for the motility and migration of different cancer cells, yet its direct role in the regulation of the polarized phenotype of the cells and actin cytoskeleton is lacking.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous studies and the current work.

claims.claim: Endogenous ERK3 co-localized to the F-actin-rich protrusions in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs).
claims.source: Endogenous ERK3 co-localized to the F-actin-rich protrusions in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs) (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Depletion of ERK3 reduced speed and displacement length of MDA-MB231 cells.
claims.source: Depletion of ERK3 reduced speed and displacement length (distance between the start point and the end position of the cell along each axis) of MDA-MB231 cells (Figure 1B–F and Videos 1–4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell tracking data shown in Figure 1B-F.

claims.claim: Depletion of ERK3 strongly reduced random cell motility.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1C, depletion of ERK3 strongly reduced random cell motility, which remained low over time, as indicated by the calculated acceleration (Figure 1D) and concomitantly resulted in a shorter overall displacement length (Figure 1E) with shorter migration track length and average speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Intravital imaging of the orthotopic mammary tumors confirmed reduced motility of the ERK3 knockdown MDA-MB231-GFP cells.
claims.source: Intravital imaging of the orthotopic mammary tumors confirmed reduced motility of the ERK3 knockdown MDA-MB231-GFP cells (Figure 1G and Videos 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 1G and Videos 5 and 6.

claims.claim: Knockdown of ERK3 significantly attenuated the EGF-induced chemotaxis of both HMECs and metastatic MDA-MB231 cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, knockdown of ERK3 significantly attenuated the EGF-induced chemotaxis of both cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F, respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-F.

claims.claim: EGF induced serine 189 (S189) phosphorylation of ERK3 at early time points in primary epithelial cells.
claims.source: EGF induced serine 189 (S189) phosphorylation of ERK3 at early time points in primary epithelial cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) and MDA-MB231 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D.

claims.claim: EGF treatment did not increase ERK3 protein half-life.
claims.source: Further cycloheximide (CHX) chase experiments coupled with RT-PCR analyses suggested that EGF treatment did not increase ERK3 protein half-life (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–2H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CHX chase and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-2H.

claims.claim: Knockdown of ERK3 clearly reduced F-actin content and actin-rich protrusions in human mammary primary epithelial cells.
claims.source: Moreover, knockdown of ERK3 clearly reduced F-actin content and actin-rich protrusions in human mammary primary epithelial cells (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: ERK3-depleted cells had limited, diffuse F-actin, concentrated in the cortical areas of the cells, and a significantly decreased number of filopodia.
claims.source: Further analyses of control and ERK3 knockdown HMECs at the single-cell level confirmed that ERK3-depleted cells had limited, diffuse F-actin, concentrated in the cortical areas of the cells, and a significantly decreased number of filopodia (Figure 1G–J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal and SEM imaging data shown in Figure 1G-J.

claims.claim: EGF signaling triggers activation of RAC1 and CDC42.
claims.source: EGF signaling triggers activation of RAC1 and CDC42, which link the signal to the actin cytoskeleton leading to the formation of lamellipodia- and filopodia-like protrusions, respectively (Figure 2A; Kurokawa et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kurokawa et al., 2004 and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: ERK3 knockdown significantly decreased the levels of both basal and EGF-induced GTP-bound CDC42 and RAC1 in primary (HMEC) and triple-negative breast cancer (MDA-MB231) mammary epithelial cells.
claims.source: ERK3 knockdown significantly decreased the levels of both basal and EGF-induced GTP-bound CDC42 and RAC1 in primary (HMEC) (Figure 2B, D, and F) and triple-negative breast cancer (MDA-MB231) mammary epithelial cells (Figure 2C, E, and G), respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2B-G.

claims.claim: ERK3 protein co-precipitated with the active RhoGTPases at endogenous levels.
claims.source: Intriguingly, we could observe co-precipitation of ERK3 protein with the active RhoGTPases at endogenous levels, suggesting that these proteins exist in a multimeric complex (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claims.claim: Depletion of ERK3 reduced the activity of RAC1 and CDC42 in multiple cell types.
claims.source: We expanded these analyses to different cell types and consistently found that depletion of ERK3 reduced the activity of RAC1 and CDC42 and that the active RhoGTPases specifically co-precipitated endogenous ERK3 (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claims.claim: ERK3 directly bound to RAC1 and CDC42 in a nucleotide-independent manner.
claims.source: By employing purified full-length recombinant proteins, we found that ERK3 directly bound to RAC1 and CDC42 in a nucleotide-independent manner (Figure 2H and I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro GST pull-down data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claims.claim: Binding of full-length ERK3 to RAC1 and CDC42 could be detected at a low nanomolar range (5 nM).
claims.source: Binding of full-length ERK3 to RAC1 and CDC42 could be detected at a low nanomolar range (5 nM) (Figure 2J and K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2J and K.

claims.claim: The kinase domain of ERK3 was sufficient for its binding to RAC1 and CDC42.
claims.source: In vitro GST-pull-down assays confirmed that the kinase domain of ERK3 was sufficient for its binding to RAC1 and CDC42 (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The ERK3 kinase domain stimulated GDP-GTP exchange on CDC42.
claims.source: These experiments showed that although ERK3 regulated the activity of both CDC42 and RAC1 in cultured cells, it only directly stimulated the GDP-GTP exchange of CDC42 (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro GDP-GTP exchange assay data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: ERK3 did not directly stimulate the GDP-GTP exchange of RAC1.
claims.source: These experiments showed that although ERK3 regulated the activity of both CDC42 and RAC1 in cultured cells, it only directly stimulated the GDP-GTP exchange of CDC42 (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro GDP-GTP exchange assay data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: Addition of ERK3 stimulated GTP-loading on CDC42 in a fluorophore-based assay.
claims.source: The results confirmed those of the previous assay as addition of ERK3 stimulated GTP-loading on CDC42 (Figure 3F) but not on RAC1 (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorophore-based GEF activity assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: ERK3 exerted a more potent and long-lasting effect than Dbl's Big Sister (Dbs) on CDC42 activation.
claims.source: Notably, ERK3 exerted a more potent and long-lasting effect than Dbl's Big Sister (Dbs), a well-established GEF for CDC42 and RhoA proteins (Figure 3F; Baumeister et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorophore-based GEF activity assay data shown in Figure 3F and a citation to Baumeister et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Full-length ERK3 exhibited weaker GEF activity in vitro than the kinase domain of ERK3.
claims.source: Interestingly, full-length ERK3 exhibited weaker GEF activity in vitro than the kinase domain of ERK3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GEF activity assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Knockdown of ERK3 does not disrupt the localization of CDC42 and RAC1 to the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Cellular fractionation assays revealed that knockdown of ERK3 does not disrupt the localization of CDC42 and RAC1 to the PM (Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claims.claim: The plasma membrane fraction from ERK3-depleted HMECs had more total CDC42 and RAC1 than control cells.
claims.source: On the contrary, the PM fraction from ERK3-depleted HMECs had more total CDC42 and RAC1 than control cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Although both RhoGTPases are present at the plasma membrane in the absence of ERK3, their activity is significantly reduced.
claims.source: Interestingly, subsequent pull-down of active CDC42/RAC1 from the PM fraction revealed that although both RhoGTPases are present at the plasma membrane in the absence of ERK3, their activity is significantly reduced (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data from plasma membrane fractions shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: ERK3 colocalized with CDC42 to the protrusions at the leading edge of the cell.
claims.source: These results were corroborated by the colocalization of ERK3 with CDC42 to the protrusions at the leading edge of the cell (Figure 4D–G) with mean Pearson's correlation coefficient (PCC (r)) of 0.6638 ± 0.02946 and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (SRCC (ρ)): 0.7122 ± 0.02586 (Figure 4F and G, respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and colocalization analysis data shown in Figure 4D-G.

claims.claim: ARP2/3 complex subunits ARP3, ARP2, and ARPC1A co-precipitated with active RAC1/CDC42 along with ERK3.
claims.source: Interestingly, we readily detected the ARP2/3 complex subunits ARP3, ARP2, and ARPC1A, as well as ERK3 by immunoblots in active RAC1/CDC42 pull-downs (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Knockdown of ERK3 by CRISPR/Cas9 or with si/shRNAs led to a reduction in F-actin staining in mammary epithelial cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the reduction in active RAC1 and CDC42 levels, we observed that knockdown of ERK3 by CRISPR/Cas9 or with si/shRNAs led to a reduction in F-actin staining in mammary epithelial cells as shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Knockdown of ERK3 significantly shifted total F-actin to G-actin in both primary HMECs and MDA-MB231 cancer cells.
claims.source: Knockdown of ERK3 significantly shifted total F-actin to G-actin in both primary HMECs (Figure 5D and E) and MDA-MB231 cancer cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 5D-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claims.claim: In the absence of CDC42, colocalization between endogenous ERK3 and the ARP3 subunit of the ARP2/3 complex could still be detected.
claims.source: Moreover, in the absence of CDC42, we could still detect colocalization between endogenous ERK3 and the ARP3 subunit of the ARP2/3 complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and colocalization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D.

claims.claim: Recombinant ERK3 stimulated ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization at a nanomolar concentration (5 nM) in the presence of 10 nM of the ARP2/3 complex.
claims.source: Indeed, recombinant ERK3 stimulated ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization at a nanomolar concentration (5 nM) in the presence of 10 nM of the ARP2/3 complex (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pyrene-actin polymerization assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The nucleation-promoting activity of ERK3 was comparable to WASP (VCA).
claims.source: Moreover, the nucleation-promoting activity of ERK3 was comparable to WASP (VCA), a well-known NPF.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pyrene-actin polymerization assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: ERK3 protein alone did not exert any stimulatory effect on actin nucleation.
claims.source: ERK3 protein alone did not exert any stimulatory effect on actin nucleation (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pyrene-actin polymerization assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Full-length ERK3 bound to the ARP2/3 complex with high-affinity in vitro.
claims.source: Indeed, using quantitative ELISAs we found that full-length ERK3 bound to the ARP2/3 complex with high-affinity in vitro (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: ERK3 directly binds to ARP3 in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.source: Through GST pull-down experiments with purified recombinant proteins, we could indeed detect a concentration-dependent direct binding between full-length ERK3 and ARP3 (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Full-length ERK3 binds to ARP3 with high affinity.
claims.source: These results were further confirmed with ELISA analyses suggesting a high-affinity binding between these two proteins (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: ERK3 co-precipitated with ARP3 and ARP2 in HMECs at endogenous levels.
claims.source: Finally, we also detected ERK3 co-precipitating with ARP3 and ARP2 in HMECs at endogenous levels (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of ARP3 at serine 418 (S418) was detected by mass spectrometry after in vitro kinase assay with ERK3.
claims.source: Initial analyses detected phosphorylation of the ARP3 subunit at serine 418 (S418) (peptide sequence: HNPVFGVMS, please see Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data after in vitro kinase assay.

claims.claim: Expression of the phosphorylation-mimicking ARP3 mutant (S418D) predominantly induced actin filament formation.
claims.source: Strikingly, expression of the phosphorylation-mimicking ARP3 mutant (S418D) under these settings predominantly induced actin filament formation, as indicated by the intense phalloidin staining (Figure 6F) and enhanced the F/G-actin ratio in primary mammary epithelial cells (Figure 6I and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 6F, I, and J.

claims.claim: S418D-overexpressing cells exhibited F-actin-rich protrusions.
claims.source: Moreover, S418D-overexpressing cells exhibited F-actin-rich protrusions (Figure 6F, lower panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Cells expressing non-phosphorylatable ARP3 (ARP3 S418A) had no significant effect on overall F-actin levels.
claims.source: Quantification of the F-actin levels revealed that despite the morphological distortion, cells expressing non-phosphorylatable ARP3 (ARP3 S418A) had no significant effect on overall F-actin levels (Figure 6I and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claims.claim: Knockdown of ERK3 led to a significant reduction of the F-actin levels in the ARP3 S418D-overexpressing cells.
claims.source: Knockdown of ERK3 led to a significant reduction of the F-actin levels in the ARP3 S418D-overexpressing cells (Figure 6K–M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 6K-M.

claims.claim: Knockdown of ERK3 in ARP3 S418D-overexpressing cells revealed a significant decrease in RAC1 activity, with almost no effect on CDC42.
claims.source: A concomitant active RAC1/CDC42 pull-down revealed a significant decrease in RAC1 activity, with almost no effect on CDC42 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: Significant colocalization between endogenous ERK3 and ARP3 was observed in HMECs.
claims.source: Using immunofluorescence analysis, we observed significant colocalization between endogenous ERK3 and ARP3 in HMECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and colocalization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Depletion of ERK3 reduced the migration of ARP3 S418D-expressing cells.
claims.source: Further, depletion of ERK3, as expected, reduced the migration of ARP3 S418D-expressing cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G and H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2G and H.

claims.claim: Knockdown of ERK3 led to a decrease in actin-rich protrusions and overall F-actin staining.
claims.source: Knockdown of ERK3 led to a decrease in actin-rich protrusions and overall F-actin staining (Figure 7B) with concomitant decrease in F-actin abundance (Figure 7C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claims.claim: Complementation with ERK3 WT rescued overall F-actin levels and the protrusive phenotype of the HMECs.
claims.source: Complementation with ERK3 WT rescued overall F-actin levels and the protrusive phenotype of the HMECs (Figure 7B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claims.claim: KD ERK3 recovered cytoskeletal F-actin levels to the same extent as ERK3 WT.
claims.source: Interestingly, KD ERK3 recovered cytoskeletal F-actin levels to the same extent as ERK3 WT (Figure 7C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claims.claim: Although the abundance of F-actin is rescued upon KD ERK3 overexpression, cells formed a dense meshwork of actin membrane ruffles which did not protrude into filopodia.

claims.source: These data suggest that perhaps ERK3 binding to ARP2/3 and possibly other hitherto unknown factors per se contribute to actin polymerization, while its kinase activity is probably still required for ARP2/3-dependent and CDC42-induced filopodia formation, polarization, and migration of mammalian epithelial cells.

results.result: ERK3 is required for cell motility and migration in mammary epithelial cells. Depletion of ERK3 reduced speed, displacement length, and random cell motility in MDA-MB231 cells both in vitro and in vivo (orthotopic tumors), and attenuated EGF-induced chemotaxis in both HMECs and MDA-MB231 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 and C7 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (live-cell tracking, intravital imaging, chemotaxis assays) demonstrating that ERK3 depletion consistently reduces cell motility and migration across different cell types and experimental contexts. The data include appropriate controls and quantification with statistical significance.

results.result: EGF induces S189 phosphorylation of ERK3 at early time points in epithelial cells, but does not increase ERK3 protein half-life.
results.evaluation: Claims C37 and C38 are supported by western blot analyses showing EGF-induced phosphorylation and CHX chase experiments demonstrating no change in protein stability. The experiments include appropriate time courses and controls.

results.result: ERK3 is required for F-actin content and filopodia formation in mammary epithelial cells. Knockdown of ERK3 reduced F-actin content, actin-rich protrusions, and filopodia number in HMECs.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C40, C6, and C5 are supported by multiple imaging modalities (confocal microscopy, SEM) and biochemical assays (F/G-actin ratios) showing consistent effects of ERK3 depletion on actin organization. Quantification is provided with statistical significance.

results.result: ERK3 is required for activation of RAC1 and CDC42 in multiple cell types. ERK3 knockdown significantly decreased both basal and EGF-induced GTP-bound CDC42 and RAC1 in primary and cancer mammary epithelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C44, and C4 are supported by pull-down assays across multiple cell types (HMECs, MDA-MB231, MCF7, MDA-MB468, Calu1, HT-29, HUVECs) showing consistent reduction in active RhoGTPases upon ERK3 depletion. The experiments include appropriate controls and quantification.

results.result: ERK3 co-precipitates with active RhoGTPases at endogenous levels, suggesting these proteins exist in a multimeric complex.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing ERK3 in complex with active CDC42 and RAC1. However, the claim that they exist in a "multimeric complex" is somewhat inferential and would benefit from additional structural or biochemical characterization.

results.result: ERK3 directly binds to RAC1 and CDC42 in a nucleotide-independent manner with high affinity (low nanomolar range). The kinase domain of ERK3 is sufficient for binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by in vitro binding assays (GST pull-down, ELISA) using purified recombinant proteins. The nucleotide-independence is demonstrated by testing GDP- and GTP-loaded forms. Binding affinity measurements are quantitative.

results.result: ERK3 functions as a GEF specifically for CDC42 but not RAC1. The ERK3 kinase domain stimulated GDP-GTP exchange on CDC42 in vitro using two independent assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 and C2 are supported by two independent in vitro GEF assays (pull-down-based and fluorophore-based) showing ERK3 stimulates nucleotide exchange on CDC42 but not RAC1. The specificity is clearly demonstrated, and ERK3's activity is comparable to or exceeds the positive control (Dbs).

results.result: ERK3 exerted a more potent and long-lasting effect than Dbs on CDC42 activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by direct comparison in the fluorophore-based GEF assay (Figure 3F). However, the comparison is qualitative rather than quantitative (no kinetic parameters calculated), and the biological significance of this difference is unclear.

results.result: Full-length ERK3 exhibited weaker GEF activity in vitro than the kinase domain of ERK3.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 is supported by experimental data, but the authors acknowledge this may be due to differences in posttranslational modifications between the two recombinant proteins (different expression systems). This technical artifact limits interpretation of the biological significance.

results.result: ERK3 is required for RhoGTPase activity at the plasma membrane but not for their localization. Knockdown of ERK3 does not disrupt CDC42/RAC1 localization to the plasma membrane, but significantly reduces their activity there.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by cellular fractionation experiments showing that total CDC42/RAC1 levels at the plasma membrane are maintained (or increased) in ERK3-depleted cells, but their activity is significantly reduced. This distinguishes ERK3's role in activation from localization.

results.result: ERK3 colocalizes with CDC42 at cell protrusions with high correlation coefficients (PCC ~0.66, SRCC ~0.71).
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantitative colocalization analysis. The correlation coefficients indicate moderate to strong colocalization, consistent with functional interaction at these sites.

results.result: ARP2/3 complex subunits co-precipitate with active RAC1/CDC42 along with ERK3.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing ARP2/3 subunits in complex with active RhoGTPases and ERK3. This suggests a functional complex linking RhoGTPase activation to actin nucleation.

results.result: ERK3 depletion reduces F-actin levels and shifts the F-actin/G-actin ratio toward G-actin in mammary epithelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C58 and C59 are supported by confocal imaging and biochemical F/G-actin assays in both primary HMECs and MDA-MB231 cells. Multiple knockdown approaches (CRISPR, siRNA, shRNA) show consistent effects.

results.result: ERK3 and ARP3 colocalize even in the absence of CDC42.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by immunofluorescence data in CDC42-depleted cells. This suggests ERK3-ARP2/3 interaction is independent of CDC42, supporting a direct regulatory relationship.

results.result: ERK3 stimulates ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization in vitro at nanomolar concentrations, with activity comparable to WASP (VCA). ERK3 alone does not stimulate actin nucleation.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 and C9 are supported by pyrene-actin polymerization assays showing ERK3 enhances ARP2/3-dependent polymerization but has no effect without ARP2/3. The activity is comparable to the established NPF WASP (VCA), supporting a role as a nucleation-promoting factor.

results.result: ERK3 directly binds to the ARP2/3 complex and specifically to ARP3 with high affinity. This interaction occurs at endogenous levels in cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 and C8 are supported by multiple binding assays (ELISA, GST pull-down) with purified proteins and co-immunoprecipitation at endogenous levels. The binding is concentration-dependent and high-affinity.

results.result: ERK3 phosphorylates ARP3 at serine 418 (S418).
results.evaluation: Claims C68 and C3 are supported by mass spectrometry identification of the phosphorylation site after in vitro kinase assay, and by detection of S418 phosphorylation in cells using a phospho-specific antibody. The antibody specificity is validated using S418A and S418D mutants.

results.result: Expression of phospho-mimicking ARP3 (S418D) induces actin filament formation and F-actin-rich protrusions, suggesting S418 phosphorylation promotes actin polymerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C69, C70, and C93 are supported by confocal imaging and F/G-actin assays showing that S418D expression enhances F-actin levels and protrusion formation. However, the claim that phosphorylation "promotes" polymerization is somewhat inferential from the phospho-mimetic data.

results.result: Non-phosphorylatable ARP3 (S418A) has no significant effect on overall F-actin levels despite causing morphological changes.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by F/G-actin assay data showing no significant change in F-actin levels with S418A expression. This suggests S418 phosphorylation is not absolutely required for F-actin maintenance, distinguishing it from ERK3's overall requirement.

results.result: ERK3 depletion reduces F-actin levels in ARP3 S418D-overexpressing cells and decreases RAC1 activity with minimal effect on CDC42.
results.evaluation: Claims C72 and C73 are supported by F/G-actin assays and pull-down assays in the S418D background. This suggests that while S418 phosphorylation contributes to actin polymerization, ERK3 has additional functions beyond this phosphorylation event.

results.result: ERK3 colocalizes with ARP3 in cells and is required for migration of ARP3 S418D-expressing cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C74 and C75 are supported by immunofluorescence colocalization analysis and Transwell migration assays. These data support the functional relevance of the ERK3-ARP3 interaction.

results.result: ERK3 kinase activity is required for formation of actin-rich protrusions but not for F-actin polymerization per se. Kinase-dead ERK3 rescues F-actin levels but produces abnormal membrane ruffles instead of filopodia.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79, C10, and C94 are supported by complementation experiments showing that kinase-dead ERK3 rescues F-actin levels but not proper protrusion morphology. This distinguishes kinase-dependent (protrusion formation) from kinase-independent (actin polymerization) functions of ERK3.

results.result: ERK3 kinase activity does not affect ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by pyrene-actin assays comparing wild-type and kinase-dead ERK3. This is consistent with the in vivo data showing kinase-independent effects on F-actin levels.

results.result: ERK3 kinase activity is not required for CDC42 activation but is partially required for RAC1 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C81 and C82 are supported by pull-down assays in cells reconstituted with wild-type or kinase-dead ERK3. This differential requirement suggests distinct mechanisms for regulating the two RhoGTPases.

results.result: ERK3 participates in a positive feedback loop where ERK3 activates CDC42/RAC1, which activate PAKs, which in turn phosphorylate and activate ERK3.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is based on inference from the current data combined with prior knowledge about PAK-ERK3 interactions. While the individual components are supported (ERK3 activates CDC42/RAC1, PAKs phosphorylate ERK3), the feedback loop itself is not directly demonstrated and remains a model requiring further validation.

results.result: Active ERK3 kinase is required for formation of actin-regulated membrane protrusions.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 is supported by the complementation experiments with kinase-dead ERK3 showing that kinase activity is necessary for proper protrusion formation (though not for F-actin levels).

results.result: ERK3 binding to ARP2/3 contributes to actin polymerization in a kinase-independent manner, while kinase activity is required for ARP2/3-dependent and CDC42-induced filopodia formation, polarization, and migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C101 and C102 represent the authors' synthesis of the kinase-dependent and -independent functions. This is supported by the complementation experiments showing differential requirements for kinase activity in different aspects of actin regulation.

results.result: Background information on actin biology, RhoGTPases, ARP2/3 complex, and ERK3 from established literature.
results.evaluation: These claims (C11-C30, C83-C92, C95, C98-C100, C103) represent established knowledge from the literature and are appropriately cited. They provide necessary context for interpreting the novel findings.

results.result: Prior work established that ERK3 controls IL-8 production, chemotaxis, and is required for cancer cell motility and migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C31 reference prior work by the authors and others establishing ERK3's role in cell migration. These provide the foundation for the current mechanistic studies.

results.result: ERK3 acts as a direct GEF for CDC42 but not RAC1. The kinase domain of ERK3 stimulated GDP-GTP exchange on CDC42 in vitro, with activity comparable to or exceeding the established GEF Dbs, while full-length ERK3 exhibited weaker GEF activity than the kinase domain alone.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the GEF activity data (Essential revision #1 and Reviewer #3 comment #3 note 'convincing GEF assay'), but raise concerns about the high starting fluorescence in Figure 3 supplement 1 (Reviewer #3 comment #3, Essential revision #11) and request clarification about differences in activity between protein sources and whether kinase activity affects GEF function (Essential revision #3). The reviewers also request testing the kinase domain alone in cells (Essential revision #1) and testing kinase activity of the proteins used (Reviewer #2 comment #1).

results.result: ERK3 depletion prevents both basal and EGF-dependent activation of RAC1 and CDC42 in multiple cell types. ERK3 directly binds to both RAC1 and CDC42 in a nucleotide-independent manner with nanomolar affinity, and the kinase domain is sufficient for this binding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the data showing ERK3 regulates RAC1 and CDC42 activity in cells and binds directly to these GTPases. The data is described as 'compelling evidence' in the public review. Reviewers request additional experiments to understand the mechanism (Essential revisions #1-3, #10) but do not challenge the core findings.

results.result: ERK3 depletion prevents maintenance of F-actin content, filopodia formation, and epithelial cell migration. Knockdown of ERK3 reduced cell speed, displacement length, random motility, and EGF-induced chemotaxis in both primary and cancer cells, confirmed by intravital imaging in orthotopic tumors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe these results as 'very convincing' (Reviewer #1 comment #5, Essential revision #6) and note the intravital imaging data confirms reduced motility. The public review states the manuscript provides 'compelling evidence' that ERK3 is required for tumor cell motility in vivo. Reviewers request investigation of metastatic seeding (Essential revision #6) but accept the presented findings.

results.result: ERK3 binds directly to the ARP2/3 complex and ARP3 subunit with high affinity and augments ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization in vitro at nanomolar concentrations, with activity comparable to WASP (VCA). ERK3 alone does not stimulate actin nucleation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers request clarification about whether the ERK3 kinase domain is sufficient for ARP3 binding (Essential revision #2, Reviewer #3 comment #5) and whether ERK3 can bind ARP3 and CDC42 simultaneously (Reviewer #3 comment #5). The DBS isoform used needs clarification (Essential revision #5, Reviewer #1 comment #4). While the binding and polymerization data are not directly challenged, these methodological questions indicate uncertainty about the complete mechanism.

results.result: ERK3 phosphorylates ARP3 at S418, and expression of phosphorylation-mimicking ARP3 S418D induces actin filament formation and F-actin-rich protrusions. Knockdown of ERK3 reduces F-actin levels in ARP3 S418D-expressing cells and decreases RAC1 activity with minimal effect on CDC42.
results.evaluation: Reviewers request that data demonstrating ERK3 dependency for ARP3 S418 phosphorylation in cells be moved from supplement to main figure (Essential revision #4, Reviewer #2 comment #2) and that details of the ARP3 S418 antibody be provided (Essential revision #4, Reviewer #1 comment #3, Reviewer #2 comment #2). The placement in supplementary material and lack of antibody details suggest reviewers need more information to fully evaluate this claim. Reviewers also ask about actin-rich protrusions in these cells (Essential revision #7, Reviewer #2 comment #3).

results.result: ERK3 kinase activity is required for formation of actin-rich protrusions but not for overall F-actin polymerization. Kinase-dead ERK3 rescues F-actin levels but produces membrane ruffles instead of filopodia. CDC42 activation is kinase-independent while RAC1 activation is partially kinase-dependent.
results.evaluation: Reviewers emphasize the importance of Figure 7 and request moving RAC1/CDC42 activity data from supplement to main figure along with pARP3-S418 blots under different ERK3 conditions (Essential revision #10, Reviewer #3 comment #6). Reviewers note concerns about overexpressed ERK3 localization away from the actin cytoskeleton (Essential revision #13, Reviewer #3 comment #1) and request showing the V5-tag channel separately and commenting on this localization pattern. These requests indicate the mechanism of kinase-dependent vs. independent functions requires clarification.

results.result: ERK3 knockdown does not disrupt CDC42 and RAC1 localization to the plasma membrane, but their activity at the membrane is significantly reduced. ERK3 colocalizes with CDC42 at protrusions at the leading edge of cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the colocalization data is 'supportive' but lacks proper controls (Essential revision #12, Reviewer #3 comment #4) and request changing the wording from 'corroborated' to 'supported' in the results text. This indicates the colocalization evidence is viewed as weaker support for the functional relationship.

results.result: EGF induces ERK3 S189 phosphorylation at early time points in primary and cancer cells, but EGF treatment does not increase ERK3 protein half-life.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the authors 'convincingly show that EGF stim leads to pERK3-S189 phosphorylation' (Reviewer #3 comment #7) but comment that it remains unclear how this impacts pERK3-small GTPase dynamics. The data itself is accepted, though its mechanistic implications need further exploration.

results.result: ERK3 colocalizes with F-actin-rich protrusions and co-precipitates with active RhoGTPases and ARP2/3 complex subunits at endogenous levels. Colocalization between ERK3 and ARP3 persists in the absence of CDC42.
results.evaluation: These colocalization and co-immunoprecipitation data support the physical interactions between ERK3 and its binding partners. While reviewers request additional controls for some colocalization experiments (Essential revision #12), they do not challenge the existence of these interactions.

results.result: ERK3 knockdown by CRISPR/Cas9 or RNAi reduces F-actin staining and shifts F-actin to G-actin in both primary and cancer mammary epithelial cells.
results.evaluation: These data are consistent with the overall phenotype of ERK3 depletion and are not specifically questioned by reviewers. They support the main findings about ERK3's role in actin regulation.

results.result: Depletion of ERK3 reduces migration of ARP3 S418D-expressing cells.
results.evaluation: This result is noted as 'expected' in the manuscript and supports the model that ERK3 function extends beyond ARP3 phosphorylation. Reviewers do not challenge this finding.

results.result: PAK kinases phosphorylate ERK3 at S189, and the data suggest a positive feedback loop where ERK3 activates CDC42/RAC1, which then activate PAKs that phosphorylate ERK3.
results.evaluation: Reviewers request additional discussion of this feedback mechanism in the context of the summary figure (Essential revision #9, Reviewer #2 comment #5). The existence of PAK-mediated ERK3 phosphorylation is established by citations and accepted; reviewers want more discussion of its implications.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate ERK3 phosphorylation by EGF (C37, C38). OpenEval finds the data SUPPORTED with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED ('convincingly show') but note mechanistic implications remain unclear.

Both address ERK3 depletion effects on actin organization (C58, C59). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with multiple approaches and statistical significance. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, consistent with overall phenotype findings.

Both evaluate membrane localization and activity of CDC42/RAC1 (C53-C55) and colocalization (C56). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, distinguishing activation from localization. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting colocalization is 'supportive' but lacks proper controls.

Both assess ERK3 GEF activity (C2, C48-C50). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with clear specificity demonstrated. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, acknowledging 'convincing GEF assay' but raising concerns about high starting fluorescence, protein source differences, and requesting kinase activity testing.

OpenEval evaluates comparative GEF activity (C51) as SUPPORTED but notes qualitative comparison. Peer reviewers include C51 in UNCERTAIN evaluation, requesting clarification about protein source differences.

OpenEval rates C52 UNCERTAIN due to potential technical artifacts from different expression systems. Peer reviewers also include C52 in UNCERTAIN evaluation, requesting testing of kinase activity and protein source clarification.

Both evaluate ERK3 regulation of RhoGTPase activity (C4, C42, C44). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with consistent pull-down data across cell types. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED ('compelling evidence'), requesting mechanism clarification but not challenging core findings.

OpenEval evaluates direct binding to GTPases (C45-C47) as SUPPORTED with quantitative in vitro data. Peer reviewers rate overlapping claims (C45-C47 in context of C4, C42, C44) as SUPPORTED, accepting binding evidence.

Both evaluate ERK3 effects on cell motility and migration (C7, C32-C36). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with converging evidence from multiple approaches. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED ('very convincing', 'compelling evidence'), particularly noting intravital imaging confirmation.

Both address actin organization effects (C5, C6, C39, C40). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with multiple imaging modalities and quantification. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED as part of overall motility phenotype.

Both evaluate ERK3-ARP2/3 binding (C8, C64-C67). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with multiple binding assays and endogenous co-IP. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting clarification about kinase domain sufficiency and simultaneous binding capacity.

Both address ERK3 effects on actin polymerization via ARP2/3 (C9, C61-C63). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with pyrene-actin assays showing NPF activity. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting methodological clarifications about binding mechanisms.

Both evaluate ARP3 S418 phosphorylation (C3, C68). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with mass spec and phospho-specific antibody validation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting data be moved from supplement to main figure and antibody details provided.

Both address S418 phosphorylation effects on actin (C69, C70, C93). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED but notes phospho-mimetic data is somewhat inferential. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting more information about ERK3 dependency and protrusion morphology.
OpenEval evaluates S418A effects (C71) as SUPPORTED, showing phosphorylation not absolutely required. Peer reviewers include C71 in UNCERTAIN evaluation, requesting additional cellular context.
